cards.fact: He worked out the size of the Earth from one hilltop in the Punjab: first the hill's height, then how far the horizon dipped below level from its top. His answer was within about one percent of today's.
cards.art: Al-Biruni about 1020 on the flat top of a rocky hill near the fort of Nandana in the Punjab, at dawn, measuring how far the horizon dips: a lean Persian scholar of about fifty with a short graying beard and a plain white turban, in a long dark coat, kneeling on one knee behind a large brass instrument as wide as his shoulders, a quarter circle of brass marked along its curved edge, set upright on a stone, with a sighting rod pivoted at its corner that he lines up on the far horizon with one eye closed. One young assistant beside him, different in age and dress, holds a wax tablet and a pen ready to write down the angle. Behind them the hill falls away steeply, and far below lies a wide, flat, hazy plain whose edge meets the sky in a long level line, a little below the level of the brass instrument. Seen from beside the instrument, from low, so that the instrument, Al-Biruni's face and the falling hillside are all in the upper half of the picture, his head three fifths of the way across the picture and a quarter of the way down. Only two people. No telescope, no glass lenses, no globe, no modern compass, no book with a printed cover. Keep the top left corner and the top right corner of the picture plain: the card's own labels cover those two corners. Nothing round hangs or stands in those corners: no plates, dishes, bowls or medallions.
